chat_history.content: I believe there is fire in the eye reaching outward toward the visible world. If you disagree, show me why vision must travel not from eye to world, but from world to eye.
in complete darkness the eye does not light objects by itself, so vision must depend on light entering the eye from outside.

In darkness nothing appears, yet that shows the eye’s inner fire seeks light to act. Without external rays the fire cannot form images; it only rises toward the illuminated world. Thus vision is a meeting of inner flame and outer light.
very bright light can injure the eye, which shows the causal action travels into the eye rather than out from it.

Indeed, bright light can harm the eye, showing it comes inward, but that proves the eye’s inner fire draws light toward itself. Without that fire, light would pass unimpeded. Thus the fire is the source that engages the external rays.
a small opening can project an inverted image of a bright scene, which makes sense if light travels from the object toward the observer.
I see how a pinhole projects an inverted picture; it shows light enters and is guided. Yet this guiding is the eye’s inner flame, which summons the light into its own depth.
if the eye sent out the main rays, the size of an outside opening should not govern the shape of the image cast by light from the scene.

I concede that the opening limits the light that can reach the eye, but it is the eye’s inner flame that gathers and directs that light. The flame does not cast rays outward; it calls the external light inward, shaping the image within the eye.
shadows and beams show that light has a direction from source to object and then to eye, rather than springing outward from vision itself.
I admit shadows and beams are powerful, showing light moves toward the eye. Yet the eye's inner fire beckons these rays, drawing them into its own depth.
one theory explains darkness, injury, and the aperture image at once if light comes from the world into the eye.
Your claim is weak, and I reject it. Bring me something stronger.
if merely looking were enough to illuminate things, staring harder in darkness would reveal them, but experience always denies this.

I admit the observation is powerful, but I still hold that the eye’s inner fire draws light inward. The darkness persists because without the eye’s fire, external light cannot be gathered. Thus the eye’s fire remains essential.
external light accounts for both seeing and being dazzled, while eye-fire has to borrow the same facts without needing its own rays.

I concede darkness hides sight, yet that shows the eye’s fire is not a mere passenger; it summons light. The inner fire must act as a receptacle, drawing outer rays into perception. Without that, the world remains unseen.
